SB: A sinus bradycardia tracing has a sinus P wave before each QRS complex with a ventricular rate below 60 beats per minute.
The rhythm is usually regular, but the R-R intervals are longer than expected because the sinus node fires slowly.
P-wave morphology remains consistent with sinus origin despite the reduced heart rate.
The PR interval is generally stable from beat to beat in uncomplicated sinus bradycardia.
QRS complexes are commonly narrow unless a separate conduction abnormality is present.
The defining feature is a slow sinus rhythm rather than dropped beats or atrioventricular dissociation.
Lead II typically shows upright P waves preceding every conducted QRS complex.
A one-to-one P-to-QRS relationship distinguishes sinus bradycardia from many bradyarrhythmias.
The baseline between beats is usually organized without fibrillatory or flutter activity.
The ventricular response follows the atrial rhythm at the same slow rate.
Long R-R intervals occur uniformly when the rhythm is regular sinus bradycardia.
Normal sinus activation sequence is preserved even though the cycle length is prolonged.
Sinus bradycardia may retain normal QRS and T-wave morphology apart from rate-related changes.
There are no premature atrial impulses driving the rhythm in isolated sinus bradycardia.
The ECG shows organized atrial and ventricular depolarization at a rate slower than the normal adult sinus range.
Overall, sinus bradycardia is a slow but otherwise sinus-origin rhythm with a P wave before each QRS.
SR: A sinus rhythm tracing has an upright sinus P wave before every QRS complex and a consistent P-wave shape.
The atrial impulse originates from the sinus node and conducts to the ventricles in a one-to-one pattern.
R-R intervals are regular or show only mild physiologic variation.
The adult heart rate is commonly within the normal resting range of approximately 60 to 100 beats per minute.
The PR interval is stable and each P wave is followed by a QRS complex.
QRS complexes are usually narrow when no additional conduction disorder is present.
Lead II generally shows upright P waves, while aVR commonly shows negative P waves.
There is no chaotic fibrillatory baseline or repetitive flutter-wave pattern.
The rhythm has organized atrial activity followed by organized ventricular activation.
The P-P and R-R intervals follow the same underlying sinus cycle length.
The tracing lacks sustained tachycardia or clinically significant bradycardia as its defining rhythm.
No ectopic atrial focus replaces the sinus P-wave morphology in a normal sinus rhythm.
Each cardiac cycle preserves the expected P-QRS-T sequence.
The ventricular rate is controlled by regular impulses from the sinoatrial node.
Sinus rhythm can coexist with non-rhythm ECG findings, but its atrial activation remains sinus in origin.
Overall, sinus rhythm is an organized one-to-one atrioventricular rhythm generated by the sinus node.
AFIB: Atrial fibrillation shows an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm with no consistent repeating R-R pattern.
Discrete sinus P waves are absent and are replaced by disorganized atrial electrical activity.
The baseline may contain fine or coarse fibrillatory oscillations between QRS complexes.
The ventricular response varies unpredictably because atrioventricular conduction is irregular.
QRS complexes are often narrow unless a separate bundle-branch or rate-related conduction abnormality exists.
There is no stable P-to-QRS relationship in atrial fibrillation.
Beat-to-beat cycle lengths fluctuate without the grouped pattern expected from regular block.
Atrial activity is chaotic rather than the uniform sawtooth pattern of atrial flutter.
The absence of organized P waves is seen across multiple leads.
Rapid atrial activation produces variable penetration of impulses through the atrioventricular node.
The ventricular rhythm can be slow, controlled, or rapid while remaining irregularly irregular.
Fibrillatory waves may be most visible in lead V1 or the inferior leads.
No single ectopic P-wave morphology repeatedly drives the tachycardia.
Long and short R-R intervals appear in a non-periodic sequence.
The ECG demonstrates disorganized atrial depolarization with an irregular ventricular response.
Overall, atrial fibrillation is identified by absent organized P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm.
ST: Sinus tachycardia has a sinus P wave before every QRS complex with a rate above 100 beats per minute.
The rhythm is typically regular and preserves one-to-one atrioventricular conduction.
P-wave morphology remains consistent with sinus-node origin despite the accelerated rate.
The R-R intervals are shortened uniformly as the sinus cycle length decreases.
QRS complexes are generally narrow unless another conduction abnormality is present.
The onset and offset are often gradual rather than abruptly paroxysmal.
Lead II usually shows upright P waves that remain visible before each QRS at moderate rates.
The PR interval may shorten slightly with rate but stays consistent beat to beat.
There is no fibrillatory baseline or organized flutter-wave activity.
The ventricular rate follows the atrial sinus rate in a one-to-one relationship.
Sinus tachycardia maintains the normal P-QRS-T activation sequence at an accelerated pace.
At very fast rates, P waves may approach the preceding T wave but retain sinus morphology.
The rhythm lacks the abrupt reentrant pattern typical of many paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias.
Uniform sinus P waves distinguish sinus tachycardia from focal atrial tachycardia.
The ECG shows organized rapid atrial activation from the sinoatrial node.
Overall, sinus tachycardia is a regular, fast sinus-origin rhythm with a P wave before each QRS.
AF: Atrial flutter commonly shows repetitive sawtooth flutter waves caused by a rapid organized atrial circuit.
Flutter activity is often most visible in the inferior leads II, III, and aVF.
The atrial rate is typically near 250 to 350 beats per minute.
The ventricular response may be regular with fixed two-to-one, three-to-one, or four-to-one conduction.
Variable atrioventricular block can make the ventricular rhythm irregular while atrial activity remains regular.
Distinct sinus P waves are replaced by continuous organized flutter waves.
There may be little or no isoelectric baseline between successive atrial deflections.
QRS complexes are usually narrow unless an independent conduction disturbance exists.
A two-to-one conducted flutter often produces a ventricular rate near 150 beats per minute.
Atrial flutter has regular atrial cycle lengths, unlike the chaotic atrial activity of atrial fibrillation.
Flutter waves in lead V1 may appear upright while inferior-lead flutter waves are often negative in typical flutter.
The atrioventricular node determines how many organized atrial impulses reach the ventricles.
Hidden flutter waves may be embedded in the QRS or T wave when conduction is two to one.
Vagal or conduction changes can expose additional flutter waves by increasing atrioventricular block.
The ECG demonstrates a macroreentrant organized atrial rhythm with repetitive atrial deflections.
Overall, atrial flutter is recognized by rapid regular flutter waves with fixed or variable ventricular conduction.
SA: Sinus irregularity shows sinus P waves with cyclic variation in the P-P and R-R intervals.
Each P wave retains sinus morphology and is followed by a QRS complex.
The rhythm varies in rate while maintaining a sinus origin.
R-R interval changes are often gradual rather than abrupt and random.
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia commonly accelerates with inspiration and slows with expiration.
The P-wave shape remains stable despite variation in cycle length.
The PR interval is generally consistent and atrioventricular conduction remains one to one.
QRS complexes are usually narrow unless a separate conduction condition is present.
There is no absence of organized P waves as seen in atrial fibrillation.
The irregularity follows a patterned or phasic variation rather than a chaotic sequence.
No premature ectopic P wave is required to explain the changing R-R intervals.
The baseline remains organized between cardiac cycles.
Sinus pauses or marked cycle-length variation can occur while the next impulse still has sinus morphology.
P-P interval variability parallels R-R interval variability because the ventricles follow the sinus impulses.
The ECG reflects changing sinus-node automaticity rather than a reentrant tachycardia.
Overall, sinus irregularity is an irregular sinus rhythm with preserved sinus P waves and one-to-one conduction.
SVT: Supraventricular tachycardia is a rapid rhythm arising above the ventricles, usually with narrow QRS complexes.
The ventricular rhythm is commonly regular and fast, often between 150 and 250 beats per minute.
P waves may be hidden within the QRS complexes or T waves because atrial and ventricular activation are close together.
The onset and termination can be abrupt when the mechanism is reentrant.
QRS duration is usually below 120 milliseconds unless aberrant conduction is present.
Retrograde P waves may appear immediately after the QRS complex in some supraventricular tachycardias.
The R-R intervals are short and highly regular during a sustained episode.
The rhythm does not show the irregularly irregular ventricular response of atrial fibrillation.
Atrial activity is often difficult to separate from the rapid ventricular complexes.
Supraventricular tachycardia is a broad rhythm category that includes nodal, accessory-pathway, and atrial mechanisms.
Rate-related ST depression can occur during a rapid supraventricular rhythm.
A narrow-complex regular tachycardia strongly supports a supraventricular origin.
Ventricular activation generally uses the normal His-Purkinje system.
The P-to-QRS timing may be short, long, or not visibly measurable depending on the mechanism.
The ECG shows a sustained rapid organized rhythm originating above the ventricular myocardium.
Overall, supraventricular tachycardia is a fast, usually regular narrow-complex rhythm of supraventricular origin.
AT: Atrial tachycardia is driven by an ectopic atrial focus that produces P waves different from sinus P waves.
The atrial rate is usually above 100 beats per minute and the rhythm is often regular.
Abnormal P waves precede the QRS complexes when atrioventricular conduction is one to one.
There is typically an isoelectric interval between ectopic P waves, unlike continuous atrial flutter activity.
P-wave axis and shape depend on the location of the atrial focus.
The PR interval may differ from sinus rhythm but is often stable during the episode.
QRS complexes are usually narrow because ventricular conduction follows the normal His-Purkinje system.
Warm-up and cool-down behavior can occur with an automatic atrial focus.
Atrial tachycardia may show variable atrioventricular block while the atrial rhythm remains regular.
The atrial activity is organized rather than chaotic as in atrial fibrillation.
Multiple visible identical non-sinus P waves support a focal atrial source.
The R-R rhythm is regular when every atrial impulse conducts to the ventricles.
At fast rates, the ectopic P wave may overlap the preceding T wave.
The tachycardia does not require simultaneous atrioventricular nodal activation as in AVNRT.
The ECG demonstrates rapid organized atrial depolarization from a non-sinus focus.
Overall, atrial tachycardia is a regular rapid atrial rhythm with repeated abnormal P-wave morphology.
AVNRT: AV nodal reentrant tachycardia is a regular narrow-complex tachycardia caused by a reentry circuit within or near the atrioventricular node.
The onset and termination are usually abrupt.
Typical AVNRT often has a short R-P interval because atria and ventricles activate nearly simultaneously.
Retrograde P waves may be hidden inside the QRS complex.
A pseudo R-prime deflection can appear in lead V1 from retrograde atrial activation.
Pseudo S waves may appear in the inferior leads immediately after the QRS complex.
The ventricular rate is commonly between 150 and 250 beats per minute.
R-R intervals are highly regular during the tachycardia.
QRS complexes are usually narrow unless rate-related aberrancy occurs.
There is no sawtooth flutter-wave pattern and no irregularly irregular response.
Atrial activation follows or coincides with ventricular activation in typical slow-fast AVNRT.
The visible R-P interval is generally shorter than the P-R interval in typical AVNRT.
The rhythm uses dual atrioventricular nodal pathways for its reentrant circuit.
An ectopic atrial P wave does not consistently precede each QRS as it does in focal atrial tachycardia.
The ECG shows a paroxysmal, regular, short-R-P supraventricular tachycardia.
Overall, AVNRT is an abrupt regular narrow-complex tachycardia with atrial activation hidden in or just after the QRS.
AVRT: Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia uses the atrioventricular node and an accessory pathway as parts of a reentry circuit.
Orthodromic AVRT is usually a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
Retrograde P waves often follow each QRS complex because the accessory pathway conducts back to the atria.
The R-P interval is typically visible and may be longer than in typical AVNRT.
The onset and termination are commonly abrupt.
R-R intervals are highly regular during a sustained episode.
The ventricular rate often falls between 150 and 250 beats per minute.
Orthodromic conduction travels to the ventricles through the atrioventricular node and returns through the accessory pathway.
Antidromic AVRT can produce a regular wide-complex tachycardia due to antegrade accessory-pathway conduction.
Baseline preexcitation with a short PR interval and delta wave may be present but is not required between episodes.
Retrograde atrial activation can create negative P waves in inferior leads after the QRS.
The rhythm is organized and regular rather than irregularly irregular.
There is no continuous sawtooth atrial activity as in atrial flutter.
The accessory pathway provides the second limb needed to maintain the macroreentrant circuit.
The ECG shows a paroxysmal reentrant supraventricular tachycardia with a consistent QRS-to-P relationship.
Overall, AVRT is a regular reentrant tachycardia involving both the atrioventricular node and an accessory pathway.
SAAWR: A wandering atrial rhythm shows at least three different P-wave morphologies as the atrial pacemaker site shifts.
The P-wave axis and shape change from beat to beat while QRS complexes are usually narrow.
P-R intervals can vary because each atrial focus lies at a different distance from the atrioventricular node.
The ventricular rate is generally below 100 beats per minute when the rhythm is termed wandering atrial pacemaker.
R-R intervals are irregular because the atrial pacemaker location and cycle length vary.
Discrete P waves remain present, distinguishing the rhythm from atrial fibrillation.
The baseline has no continuous sawtooth flutter-wave activity.
Each conducted P wave is ordinarily followed by a QRS complex.
The varying P-wave morphologies indicate shifting atrial activation origins rather than one stable ectopic focus.
QRS morphology remains similar across beats if ventricular conduction is normal.
The rhythm may alternate between sinus-node and lower atrial pacemaker sites.
The irregularity is accompanied by visible changing P waves rather than chaotic fibrillatory activity.
A rate above 100 beats per minute with the same multiform atrial pattern would be called multifocal atrial tachycardia.
The P-P, P-R, and R-R intervals may all vary across the tracing.
The ECG demonstrates organized but migrating atrial pacemaker activity.
Overall, sinus-to-atrial wandering rhythm is an irregular rhythm with multiple distinct P-wave morphologies and preserved QRS conduction.
